slides.title: How long until your money doubles?
slides.sub: One mental math trick: the Rule of 72

slides.heading: The rule
slides.big: 72 ÷ your yearly return = years to double
body: Divide 72 by the yearly return you expect. The answer is roughly how many years it takes your money to double.

slides.heading: Try it
slides.note: Higher returns usually come with more risk.

slides.heading: Why starting early wins
slides.intro: One $1,000 deposit growing at 9% a year:

slides.takeaway: Time does the heavy lifting. Start small, but start now.

posts.caption:
Quick math trick: divide 72 by your yearly return to see how many years it takes your money to double.

At 9%, that's about 8 years. Start at 18 and a single $1,000 could grow to around $16,000 by age 50 without adding another dollar. Returns aren't guaranteed, but time is the biggest advantage you have right now.

slides.title: Paying in full isn't enough for your score
slides.sub: Why the day you pay matters, and what the newest scoring models track.

slides.heading: The balance that gets reported
body: Most card issuers report your balance to the credit bureaus on or right after your statement closing date.
Pay in full by the due date and you pay zero interest. But the bureaus already saw the full balance.

slides.heading: Same card, different timing
slides.note: FICO weighs each card on its own and your total across all cards.

slides.heading: The new twist
body: VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T look at how your balances moved over the past 24 months, not just one snapshot.
Since Sept. 2026, lenders selling mortgages to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can use VantageScore 4.0.

slides.takeaway: Pay before the statement closes, and keep it low every month.

posts.caption:
Paying your card in full every month is great. But your score may still see a high balance, because most issuers report your balance on the statement closing date, not the due date.

Example: $1,000 limit, $600 spent. Pay after the statement closes and the bureaus see 60% utilization. Pay $500 a few days before it closes and they see 10%. Same spending, same card. For context, Experian found people with an 850 score average 4% utilization, while the average American sits at 29% (June 2026 data).

The twist: newer models like VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T look at 24 months of balance trends. Since September 2026, lenders selling mortgages to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can use VantageScore 4.0. A last minute paydown tells less of the story. Low balances every month win.

slides.title: The simplest budget that actually works

slides.heading: Split your take-home pay 3 ways
items: Emergency fund, investing, paying off debt

slides.heading: Example: $800 a month
slides.note: Living at home with fewer bills? Shift some of your needs money into savings while you can.

slides.heading: $160 a month adds up
body: That's saved before earning a single dollar of interest.

slides.takeaway: Pay yourself first. Move your savings the day you get paid.

posts.caption:
Budgeting doesn't have to be complicated. Try the 50/30/20 rule: 50% of your take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings.

On $800 a month, that's $160 saved. Do that for a year and you've got $1,920 before any interest. Still living at home? Push that savings number even higher while your bills are low.

posts.caption:
An index fund lets you own a slice of the whole market in one purchase. An S&P 500 index fund holds about 500 of the biggest US companies.

The part most people miss: fees. $10,000 growing for 30 years at 7% before fees ends up around $75,500 with a 0.03% fee, but only about $57,400 with a 1% fee. That's roughly $18,000 lost to fees.

slides.title: Your 18th birthday money checklist
slides.sub: What to set up now so you start adult life with real credit.

slides.heading: Before you turn 18
items: A parent adds you to a card they pay on time. Their history can help start yours.
Practice tracking money before the bills show up.
Earned income is what lets you open a Roth IRA.

slides.heading: At 18
items: Free every week from all 3 bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com.
Under 21, you need your own income or a cosigner. Try a student or secured card.
2026 limit: $7,500, up to what you earn.

slides.heading: Why start at 18, not 28
slides.intro: Investing $100 a month at 7%, value at 65:
slides.note: 10 extra years. $12,000 more put in. About $229,000 more at 65.
slides.source: 7% yearly return is an assumption, not a guarantee.

slides.takeaway: Your credit clock starts when your first account opens. Start it on purpose.

posts.caption:
16 or 17? You've got one more year left. It's time to prepare.

Turning 18 is when your credit story can officially start. Here's the checklist:

Before 18: ask a parent to add you as an authorized user on a card they pay on time, open a checking and savings account, and get a job (earned income is what lets you open a Roth IRA).

At 18: pull your free credit reports every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, get a student or secured card (under 21 you need your own income or a cosigner), and open a Roth IRA. The 2026 limit is $7,500, up to what you earn.

Why the rush? $100 a month at 7% from age 18 grows to about $438,600 by 65. Start at 28 and it's about $209,700. Ten extra years, $12,000 more put in, about $229,000 more at the end.

slides.sub: Don't want to be a business major? These open the same doors.

slides.heading: The top five
items: Product management, tech consulting, and business analytics.
Runs operations and supply chains. Built to make companies efficient.
Models hard problems. Consulting and quant teams hire physics grads.

slides.heading: The top five
items: Data, pricing, and analytics jobs where numbers drive decisions.
Marketing, HR, and user research. Business runs on people.
slides.note: Pair any of these with a business minor or an internship and you compete with business majors.

slides.heading: The pay
slides.intro: Median yearly pay at ages 35 to 45:
slides.source: Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

slides.takeaway: You don't need a business degree to work in business. You need skills businesses pay for.

posts.caption:
Not into a business major? You can still end up running the business. Here are 5 majors that work really well in the business world (according to Claude).

1. Computer science: product management, tech consulting, business analytics
2. Industrial engineering: operations and supply chains
3. Physics: modeling hard problems, which consulting and quant teams love
4. Mathematics: data, pricing, and analytics
5. Psychology: marketing, HR, and user research

Mid-career median pay (ages 35 to 45): computer science $120,000, physics $105,000, industrial engineering and math $100,000 each, compared with $87,000 for all majors. Psychology comes in at $72,000, so pair it with a business minor or data skills.

Which major are you thinking about? Tell us in the comments.

Pay data: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates. Rankings are according to Claude.
